# summarize category
# function to summarize any categorical variable
summarize_categorical <- function(df, var) {
  df %>%
    group_by({{ var }}) %>%
    summarise(
      Count = n()
    ) %>%
    mutate(
      Percentage = round(100 * Count / sum(Count), 2)
    ) %>%
    arrange(desc(Count)) %>%
    rename(Category = {{ var }})
}

# summarize all categorical predictors
genres_summary <- summarize_categorical(netflix_clean, genres)
country_summary <- summarize_categorical(netflix_clean, country)
language_summary <- summarize_categorical(netflix_clean, language)

# combine them into one list of tables
categorical_tables <- list(
  "Genres" = genres_summary,
  "Country" = country_summary,
  "Language" = language_summary
)

# display each table neatly
for (name in names(categorical_tables)) {
  cat("\n\n")
  cat(paste0("### Table: ", name, "\n\n"))
  print(
    kable(categorical_tables[[name]],
          caption = paste("Distribution of", name),
          digits = 2) %>%
      kable_styling(full_width = FALSE, bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover"))
  )
}

#The Revenue vs Predictor scatterplots reveal severe nonlinearity for most predictors, including budget, vote count, popularity, and vote average. The fan-shaped patterns and curved relationships indicate violations of both the linearity assumption and the constant-variance assumption. Cast Count and Director Count show extremely low variation and no meaningful association with revenue. Overall, these plots justify the need for transforming the response (via Box–Cox) and for removing variables with no predictive value.

library(car)

#box cox on response gives us a rounded power of 0.12 which we can round to 0,

# transformations applied 
# TRANSFORMED PREDICTORS (based on your instruction)
netflix_clean$log_revenue <- log(netflix_clean$revenue)
netflix_clean$budget_t <- log(netflix_clean$budget)

netflix_clean$vote_average_t  <- (netflix_clean$vote_average)^2

netflix_clean$vote_count_t <- log(netflix_clean$vote_count + 1)

netflix_clean$popularity_t  <- 1 / sqrt(netflix_clean$popularity + 1)

netflix_clean$release_year_t  <- (netflix_clean$release_year)^(-3)

#define new model

model2 <- lm(log_revenue ~ budget_t + vote_average_t +
                          vote_count_t + popularity_t + release_year,
                        data = netflix_clean)

#check if violation is solved

par(mfrow = c(2, 3))

plot(netflix_clean$budget_t, model2$residuals,
     xlab = "log(Budget)",
     ylab = "Residuals",
     main = "Residuals vs log(Budget)")
abline(h = 0, col = "red")

plot(netflix_clean$vote_average_t, model2$residuals,
     xlab = "(Vote Average)^2",
     ylab = "Residuals",
     main = "Residuals vs (Vote Average)^2")
abline(h = 0, col = "red")

plot(netflix_clean$vote_count_t, model2$residuals,
     xlab = "log(Vote Count + 1)",
     ylab = "Residuals",
     main = "Residuals vs log(Vote Count)")
abline(h = 0, col = "red")

plot(netflix_clean$popularity_t, model2$residuals,
     xlab = "1 / sqrt(Popularity + 1)",
     ylab = "Residuals",
     main = "Residuals vs 1/sqrt(Popularity)")
abline(h = 0, col = "red")

plot(netflix_clean$release_year_t, model2$residuals,
     xlab = "(Release Year)^(-3)",
     ylab = "Residuals",
     main = "Residuals vs (Release Year)^(-3)")
abline(h = 0, col = "red")

#We chose not to transform Release Year. Although the Box–Cox transformation suggested a negative power (λ ≈ –3), this transformation is not meaningful because Year is a discrete, ordered variable with very limited range (2010–2025). Applying a power such as collapses the scale and produces almost no variation, which harms interpretability and contributes nothing to model fit.

#Furthermore, Release Year does not exhibit clear non-linearity or heteroskedasticity in the residual plots after transforming the response. Since predictor normality is not required in regression, and interpretability is important, we retain Release Year in its original scale.

# sample size (n) = 3527
n <- nrow(netflix_clean)
# predictors (p)  = 5  check if we should include interaction terms
p <- 5

#SST 
SST <- (n -1) * var(netflix_clean$log_revenue)
#RSS
RSS <- sum((model2$fitted.values-netflix_clean$log_revenue)^2)
#SSreg
SSreg <- SST - RSS

#Find the mean squares
MSR <-  RSS / (n-p-1)
MSreg <- SSreg / p

#Compute test statistic
F_statistic <- MSreg/MSR

#Conclusion using p-value or critical value
pf(F_statistic, p, (n-p-1), lower.tail = FALSE)
qf(0.95, p, (n-p-1))


#t-test
critical_value <- qt(0.025, n-p-1)

summary(model2)

#Since the p-value of 0 is < 0.05 and  F_statistic > critical value we reject H0 and concclude that a statistically significant linear reltionship exists for at least one predictor

#t-test on each coefficient says all are significantly related

#R^2 test concludes that 54% of variation in the response has been explained by the model 

#Partial F-test (don't need to perform cause we are not reducing any predictors)


# sample size and number of predictors
n <- nrow(netflix_clean)
p <- length(coef(model2)) - 1 

# 1. LEVERAGE (hatvalues)
hii <- hatvalues(model2)
leverage_cutoff <- 2 * (p + 1) / n
high_leverage <- which(hii > leverage_cutoff)

# 2. STANDARDIZED RESIDUALS (outliers)
ri <- rstandard(model2)
if (n < 50) {
  outlier_cutoff <- 2
} else {
  outlier_cutoff <- 4
}
outliers <- which(abs(ri) > outlier_cutoff)

# 3. COOK'S DISTANCE
Di <- cooks.distance(model2)
cooks_cutoff <- qf(0.5, df1 = p + 1, df2 = n - p - 1)
influential_cooks <- which(Di > cooks_cutoff)

# 4. DFFITS
dff <- dffits(model2)
dffits_cutoff <- 2 * sqrt((p + 1) / n)
influential_dffits <- which(abs(dff) > dffits_cutoff)

# 5. DFBETAS
dfb <- dfbetas(model2)
dfbetas_cutoff <- 2 / sqrt(n)
influential_dfbetas <- which(apply(abs(dfb) > dfbetas_cutoff, 1, any))

### OUTPUT SUMMARY
cat("\n---------- PROBLEMATIC OBSERVATION SUMMARY ----------\n")
cat("High leverage points (hii > cutoff):\n"); print(high_leverage)

cat("\nOutliers (|standardized residual| > cutoff):\n"); print(outliers)

cat("\nInfluential (Cook's Distance > F-median cutoff):\n"); print(influential_cooks)

cat("\nInfluential (|DFFITS| > cutoff):\n"); print(influential_dffits)

cat("\nInfluential (DFBETAS > cutoff for at least one coefficient):\n"); print(influential_dfbetas)

cat("\n------------------------------------------------------\n")
